config.name: Citizenship
config.title: Australian Citizenship
config.subtitle: Based on Our Common Bond
config.disclaimer: Original practice questions based on the official resource Australian Citizenship: Our Common Bond. In the real test you must also answer all five values questions correctly. Not affiliated with the Department of Home Affairs.

questions.text: Who are Australia's first peoples?
choices: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 65,000 years and have the oldest continuing cultures in the world.

questions.text: What happened on 26 January 1788?
choices: The First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove and established a British colony
questions.explanation: Captain Arthur Phillip and the First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove; 26 January is now Australia Day.

questions.text: Who commanded the First Fleet?
questions.explanation: Captain Arthur Phillip led the First Fleet and became the first Governor of the colony of New South Wales.

questions.text: What happened on 1 January 1901?
choices: The colonies united to form the Commonwealth of Australia (Federation)
Women won the right to vote
questions.explanation: On 1 January 1901 the six colonies federated to form the Commonwealth of Australia.

questions.text: Who was Australia's first Prime Minister?
questions.explanation: Edmund Barton became the first Prime Minister of Australia in 1901.

questions.text: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.explanation: Canberra, in the Australian Capital Territory, is the national capital.

questions.text: How many states does Australia have?
questions.explanation: Australia has six states (New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia and Tasmania) and two mainland territories.

questions.text: Which of these is a mainland territory of Australia?
questions.explanation: The two mainland territories are the Northern Territory and the Australian Capital Territory.

questions.text: What is the capital of Victoria?
questions.explanation: Melbourne is the capital of Victoria. Sydney is the capital of New South Wales.

questions.text: What is the capital of Western Australia?
questions.explanation: Perth is the capital of Western Australia.

questions.text: What is the capital of Queensland?
questions.explanation: Brisbane is the capital of Queensland.

questions.text: What is the capital of Tasmania?
questions.explanation: Hobart is the capital of Tasmania.

questions.text: What is the capital of South Australia?
questions.explanation: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia.

questions.text: What is the capital of the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: Darwin is the capital of the Northern Territory.

questions.text: What is Australia's national language?
questions.explanation: English is Australia's national language and part of the national identity.

questions.text: What is Australia's national flower?
questions.explanation: The golden wattle is the national floral emblem; Wattle Day is 1 September.

questions.text: What are Australia's national colours?
questions.explanation: Green and gold, the colours of the golden wattle, are Australia's national colours.

questions.text: What is the name of Australia's national anthem?
questions.explanation: "Advance Australia Fair" is the national anthem.

questions.text: Which stars appear on the Australian National Flag?
choices: The Commonwealth Star and the Southern Cross
The North Star and the Big Dipper
Six stars for the six states only
questions.explanation: The flag has the Union Jack, the seven-pointed Commonwealth Star and the Southern Cross.

questions.text: What does the Commonwealth Star on the Australian flag represent?
choices: The states and territories of the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Star has seven points: one for each state and one for the territories.

questions.text: What are the colours of the Australian Aboriginal Flag?
questions.explanation: Black represents Aboriginal people, red the earth and their spiritual relation to the land, and the yellow circle the sun.

questions.text: What are the colours of the Torres Strait Islander Flag?
questions.explanation: Green stands for the land, blue for the sea, black for the people, and the white dhari (headdress) and star are symbols of the islanders.

questions.text: What is Anzac Day?
choices: A day to celebrate the harvest
The day Australians remember those who served and died in war, on 25 April
The day the First Fleet arrived
questions.explanation: Anzac Day marks the landing of Australian and New Zealand troops at Gallipoli, Turkey, on 25 April 1915.

questions.text: Where did the Anzacs land on 25 April 1915?
questions.explanation: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps troops landed at Gallipoli during the First World War.

questions.text: When is Australia Day?
questions.explanation: Australia Day, 26 January, marks the arrival of the First Fleet at Sydney Cove in 1788.

questions.text: Which of these is a famous Australian natural landmark in the Northern Territory?
questions.explanation: Uluru, a large sandstone rock sacred to the Anangu people, is in the Northern Territory.

questions.text: Off the coast of which state is most of the Great Barrier Reef?
questions.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, lies off the Queensland coast.

questions.text: Which is Australia's largest city by population?
questions.explanation: Sydney, the capital of New South Wales, is Australia's largest city.

questions.text: What did the 1967 referendum change?
choices: It allowed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to be counted in the national census
It ended the White Australia policy
questions.explanation: More than 90 per cent of Australians voted Yes in the 1967 referendum.

questions.text: Where did the federal Parliament first meet after Federation?
questions.explanation: Parliament met in Melbourne from 1901 until it moved to Canberra in 1927.

questions.text: What type of government does Australia have?
choices: A parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy
questions.explanation: Australia is a parliamentary democracy based on the rule of law, and a constitutional monarchy.

questions.text: Who is Australia's Head of State?
questions.explanation: The King is Australia's Head of State and is represented by the Governor-General.

questions.text: Who represents the King in Australia at the national level?
choices: The Premier of New South Wales
questions.explanation: The Governor-General is appointed by the King on the advice of the Prime Minister.

questions.text: Who represents the King in each state?
questions.explanation: Each state has a Governor who represents the King.

questions.text: What does "the rule of law" mean?
choices: Police can do anything they want
All Australians are equal under the law and no one is above it
Only citizens must obey the law
questions.explanation: The rule of law means everyone, including government officials, must obey the law.

questions.text: Which of these is a freedom in Australia?
choices: Freedom to break the law if you disagree with it
Freedom to use violence against others
questions.explanation: Australians have freedom of speech, association, assembly, religion and movement, within the law.

questions.text: What does freedom of religion mean in Australia?
choices: People can follow any religion they choose, or none, as long as they obey the law
Everyone must follow the same religion
Religious laws are above Australian law
questions.explanation: Australia has no official national religion; religious practices must not break Australian laws.

questions.text: What does "a fair go" mean in Australia?
choices: Everyone deserves equal opportunity, whatever their background
People get what their family had
questions.explanation: Australians value equality of opportunity: what you achieve depends on your talents and work, not your birth.

questions.text: What does "mateship" mean to many Australians?
choices: Helping one another, especially in hard times
questions.explanation: Mateship is about helping others, especially those in need.

questions.text: Is it compulsory for Australian citizens aged 18 and over to vote in federal and state elections?
choices: Only for people born in Australia
questions.explanation: Voting is compulsory for Australian citizens aged 18 and over.

questions.text: Which of these is a responsibility of Australian citizens?
choices: Serving on a jury if called
questions.explanation: Responsibilities include obeying the law, voting, defending Australia if needed and serving on a jury if called.

questions.text: Which of these is a privilege of Australian citizenship?
questions.explanation: Citizens can apply for a passport, seek election to parliament and vote; they also have responsibilities.

questions.text: How can people peacefully express their opinions in Australia?
choices: By writing to their member of parliament, joining a peaceful protest or signing a petition
By refusing to obey any law
questions.explanation: Australians can criticise the government and campaign for change, but must do so peacefully and within the law.

questions.text: Which of these is an example of equality in Australia?
choices: Older people have more legal rights
Men and women have equal rights
Only people born in Australia can work
Men earn the right to vote first
questions.explanation: Men and women have equal rights and responsibilities, and discrimination is against the law.

questions.text: What is the Australian Constitution?
choices: A treaty with Britain about trade
The legal document that sets out the basic rules for the government of Australia
questions.explanation: The Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1901 and sets out how the federal government works.

questions.text: How can the Australian Constitution be changed?
questions.explanation: A change needs a referendum approved by a majority of voters nationally and a majority of voters in a majority of states.

questions.text: What are the two houses of the federal Parliament?
choices: The Senate and the High Court
The House of Commons and the House of Lords
The House of Representatives and the Senate
questions.explanation: The federal Parliament has two houses: the House of Representatives and the Senate.

questions.text: How is the Prime Minister chosen?
choices: The leader of the party or coalition with the majority in the House of Representatives becomes Prime Minister
The High Court chooses the Prime Minister
The King chooses the Prime Minister
The people vote for the Prime Minister directly
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister is the leader of the party or coalition with the support of most members of the House of Representatives.

questions.text: Who is the leader of a state government?
questions.explanation: The Premier leads a state government; a Chief Minister leads a territory government.

questions.text: Who is the leader of a territory government?
questions.explanation: The Northern Territory and the Australian Capital Territory are led by Chief Ministers.

questions.text: What are the three levels of government in Australia?
choices: Federal, state or territory, and local
questions.explanation: Australia has a federal government, state and territory governments, and local councils.

questions.text: Which level of government is responsible for defence?
questions.explanation: Defence, foreign affairs, immigration and currency are federal responsibilities.

questions.text: Which level of government is responsible for local roads, rubbish collection and parks?
questions.explanation: Local councils look after local matters such as rubbish collection, local roads, parks and libraries.

questions.text: Which level of government is mainly responsible for hospitals, schools and police?
questions.explanation: States and territories run schools, hospitals, police and public transport, with federal funding for some services.

questions.text: What does "separation of powers" mean?
choices: Power is divided between the legislative, executive and judicial branches
questions.explanation: Dividing power between parliament, the executive government and the courts stops any one group having too much power.

questions.text: Which branch of government makes the laws?
questions.explanation: Parliament has legislative power: it makes and changes laws.

questions.text: Which branch of government interprets and applies the law?
questions.explanation: The courts are independent of the government and apply the law.

questions.text: What is the highest court in Australia?
choices: The Supreme Court of New South Wales
questions.explanation: The High Court interprets the Constitution and is the highest court of appeal.

questions.text: What is a referendum?
choices: A vote by the people to approve a change to the Constitution
An election for the Prime Minister
questions.explanation: Changes to the Constitution can only be made by referendum.

questions.text: Which of these is a federal government responsibility?
questions.explanation: Currency, defence, foreign affairs, immigration and taxation are federal matters.

questions.text: In Australia, is it acceptable to use violence against people because of their religion?
choices: No, violence against any person is against the law
Yes, if your religion allows it
questions.explanation: Australians reject the use of violence to change someone's mind; violence against people is a crime.

questions.text: Can a person be refused a job in Australia because they are a woman?
choices: Yes, if the employer prefers men
No, discrimination on the basis of sex is against the law
questions.explanation: Equality of opportunity means people cannot be treated unfairly because of their sex, race, religion or background.

questions.text: Which statement about Australian law is correct?
choices: People from other countries follow their own country's laws
Religious laws are above Australian laws
Laws apply equally to everyone, and religious laws have no legal status
Politicians do not have to follow the law
questions.explanation: Everyone must follow Australian laws; religious and cultural practices must stay within the law.

questions.text: In Australia, can people choose who they marry?
choices: Yes, and forced marriage is a crime
questions.explanation: People in Australia are free to choose whether to marry and who to marry; forced marriage is illegal.

questions.text: Which of these shows respect for Australian values?
choices: Refusing to work with people of other religions
Using threats to win an argument
Treating all people with respect, whatever their background
questions.explanation: Australia's values include respect for the equal worth, dignity and freedom of every person.

questions.text: Why is it important to learn English in Australia?
choices: It is required to vote in local elections only
It is required to keep your religion
Only English speakers can own property
It helps people take part fully in Australian life and work
questions.explanation: English is the national language and helps new citizens join in Australian society.
